The goal is Israel's destruction." "Only when they understand that, that it's hopeless for them to destroy the Jewish state of Israel, only then might they finally lay down their arms and say, we give up."

articles.title: Photos show aftermath of riots as masked groups clash with police across France
articles.summary: Paris streets littered with burned cars and shattered storefronts as police report 1,800 arrests nationwide following violent clashes over living costs.
articles.body: Paris woke Sunday to shattered storefronts, burned cars and a heavy police presence after unrest swept through the city and other parts of France. Violent clashes broke out Saturday during nationwide demonstrations over rising living costs and poor school conditions. Hundreds of thousands marched across the country, while masked groups fought with police, looted businesses and set fires in several cities. Police reported 1,800 arrests nationwide, including 855 in the Paris region. VIOLENCE ERUPTS AT FRANCE PROTESTS AS MACRON WARNS UNREST IS BEING EXPLOITED The destruction was not limited to Paris. In Limoges, about three hours south of the capital, fire tore through the city’s historic town hall, built in 1883 and designated a historic landmark in 1975. The local prefect, Maurice Barate, told AFP that the roof had collapsed onto the lower floors and about two-thirds of the building’s exterior had disappeared. He called it "a catastrophe for heritage." LIMOGES TOWN HALL ‘LARGELY LOST’ AFTER FAR-LEFT RIOTERS SET HISTORIC BUILDING ON FIRE French President Emmanuel Macron had called for "calm and respect" ahead of Saturday’s demonstrations, saying the right to protest must be exercised with respect for people and property. But as violence escalated, the French president and his wife, Brigitte, were spotted at a Celine Dion concert in Nanterre, west of Paris, according to French media reports. The couple reportedly arrived and left discreetly and joined roughly 35,000 spectators at the Plenitude Arena. Macron had spent Thursday and Friday in Brussels for a European Council meeting. WHERE'S MACRON? articles.title: I worked for 3 White House press secretaries — here’s some advice for the next one
articles.summary: Former Reagan White House staffer Mark Weinberg offers advice to the incoming U.S. press secretary by reflecting on the lessons learned from predecessors Jim Brady, Larry Speakes, and Marlin Fitzwater.
articles.body:
The U.S. has just watched the shortest press secretary tenure in its history: five days. Soon, someone new will stand at that podium, stepping into one of the hardest jobs in American public life — and a workplace unlike any other, because the room is named for a predecessor who nearly died doing it: the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room.

Jim Brady was a man I knew and loved. I served eight years in the Reagan White House press office. Three men held that podium in my time there, and each taught me something every press secretary needs.

Brady taught me that the press is not the enemy — it is the instrument. He held the job only ten weeks before a bullet meant for President Reagan changed his life forever, but his influence outlasted everyone’s. He was quick, funny, and utterly without pretense. The reporters who sparred with him adored him, because he understood that the briefing room is where the government explains itself to the governed, and the people asking the questions are how the explaining gets done. You can joust with the press all day; Brady did, happily. You cannot despise them without despising the arrangement itself.

A detail of history: after the shooting, President Reagan never gave Brady’s title away. For nearly eight years, Larry Speakes and then Marlin Fitzwater did the job under other titles, because “press secretary” belonged to Brady until the day the administration ended. That was loyalty — and a lesson: The job is bigger than its occupant.

Larry Speakes taught me the grind. He took the podium on the worst afternoon of the Reagan presidency — March 30, 1981, with the president in surgery and the world demanding answers — then did it for six more years. From Speakes I learned that the briefing is won in the hours before it: the morning papers, the overnight cables, the calls to every corner of the building to find out what was true before someone asked. The podium punishes the unprepared, and no amount of charm survives a guess.

Fitzwater taught me that all you have is your credibility — and that it is spent in a single transaction. He served two presidents of very different temperaments, and the press corps trusted him through both, for one reason: He never lied to them. When he couldn’t say, he said he couldn’t say. The result was that the president’s most loyal defender was also the man reporters believed — which is precisely what made his defense worth anything. A press secretary who will say anything is, professionally speaking, mute.

Here is the structural truth nobody explains on the first day: the job serves three masters. The president, who deserves a vigorous advocate. The press, who are owed straight answers on behalf of their readers. And the public, who own the presidency and are the actual audience for every word said from that podium. The three pull in different directions daily — and the only thing that lets one person serve all three is credibility. Your believability is not your asset; it is the president’s. Spend it never.

So, here is some counsel across the generations for the next press secretary, offered with genuine goodwill. Brief often — the room exists to be used. Prepare like Speakes; the questions are not the test, the facts are.

Never guess, and when you’re wrong, correct fast and plainly. Expect to learn more from the reporters than they learn from you — the good ones have covered that building longer than most of us worked in it; that’s how every press secretary starts. Be the president’s supporter — that is the job — but a supporter is not a sycophant, and the difference is the whole value of the role: an echo persuades no one, while an advocate who is believed is worth divisions. And this, from one communicator to another: Many Americans don’t love the press, and that’s fine. But never be rude to reporters on camera as a performance — contempt manufactured for the clip, to gain favor with anyone, demeans the room, and the room remembers. So does the country.

One more thing about the name on the door. Brady gave the job his body and never got to do it at full strength. The room was named to honor what he represented: the belief that the presidency explains itself — cheerfully, combatively, honestly — to a free press, because the presidency belongs to the public. I would offer this standard to any press secretary of any party, word for word, and I have no doubt Brady would too. The podium is not a shield and not a weapon. It is a promise.

To whoever takes the podium next: Welcome to the hardest job in the building. Good luck. The name on the room will be watching. It is a friendly gaze — and an exacting one.

Mark Weinberg, founder of the executive communications consultancy Ethos, served in the Reagan White House press office for eight years and later as a speechwriter for President Reagan. He is the author of the bestselling book “Movie Nights with the Reagans.” .

articles.title: Trump announces plans to renovate D.C. golf course amid legal battle
articles.summary: President Donald Trump announced Sunday that the administration has developed a plan to redevelop a golf course in Washington, D.C., which has been at the center of a legal battle
articles.body: President Donald Trump announced in a Truth Social post on Sunday that the administration has developed a plan to redevelop the East Potomac Golf Links course in Washington, D.C., which has been at the center of a legal battle over his renovation plans. Trump said that the Interior Department worked with golf course architect Tom Fazio to develop “a plan to build a World Class Championship Golf Course on the site of the current East Potomac Golf Links, located in Washington, D.C.” “When completed, it will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments such as the U.S. Open, the PGA Championship, the Ryder Cup, and the Presidents Cup,” Trump said in the post. He said that the renovations would begin on Nov. 15 and take about 15 months. The proposed renovation, though, has already been challenged in court by a preservation group and two D.C. residents. Last week, U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes forbade the administration from cutting down more trees at the course through Oct. 26. The administration had cut down hundreds of trees from the course, causing Reyes to hit back, saying she was “furious.” “I was hearing from everyone on plaintiffs’ side this was going to happen. I said repeatedly, ‘No, I trust the government.’ I trusted you all not to do precisely what you have done,” Reyes responded at the time. She also said that incident “cost the government all of its credibility.” Reyes said that the administration must provide her and the plaintiffs three business days’ written advance notice before making any “irreparable modification” to the golf course. The judge previously rejected the plaintiffs’ request for a restraining order because lawyers for the Trump administration said they would provide ample notice of large-scale work. National Park Service officials told Reyes last week that they were aware of no formal plan to renovate East Potomac beyond what they saw from Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and Trump’s previous social media posts. On Friday, the administration asked Reyes to recuse herself from the case, arguing that her “histrionics in prior hearings have clearly demonstrated she is no longer impartial.” The judge will hold a hearing Monday in which she has called on the acting director of the National Park Service and the Interior Department’s chief of staff to testify under oath. In Sunday’s Truth Social post, Trump said that the “current Course is old, broken, dilapidated, and of no further use or effect.” The golf course renovation is the latest in a string of major changes the president has tried to make to the D.C. landscape. He is continuing to build the White House ballroom and has pushed forward on plans to build a “triumphal arch.” His handpicked Kennedy Center board also voted to close the renowned arts center for renovations, and the administration moved to renovate the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, though the lining ended up peeling.

articles.title: Massachusetts Republican lieutenant governor candidate suspends campaign after OUI arrest
articles.summary: Shawn Oliver, a Republican candidate for lieutenant governor of Massachusetts, suspended his campaign after he was arrested on drunken driving charges following a crash late Saturday that left several parked vehicles damaged and his own overturned.
articles.body: A candidate for lieutenant governor of Massachusetts, Republican Shawn Oliver, was arrested on drunken driving charges after a crash late Saturday that left several parked vehicles damaged and his own overturned, police said. On Sunday, Oliver, a city councilor in New Bedford, announced he was suspending his campaign, as his running mate, Mike Minogue, had called for him to do. “After careful reflection, I have made the decision to suspend my campaign for Lieutenant Governor,” Oliver said in a statement. “This election is too important to be overshadowed by personal matters. I want to sincerely thank everyone who has supported me throughout this journey and ask that my family’s privacy be respected during this difficult time.” He faces charges of operating under the influence of liquor, negligent operation of a motor vehicle, a marked lanes violation and speeding, New Bedford police said Sunday. They said Oliver’s vehicle overturned after hitting five parked vehicles, two of which were extensively damaged, near a shopping plaza on Dartmouth Street about 11:40 p.m. The candidate was taken to St. Luke’s Hospital to be treated and was later arrested. It wasn’t immediately clear if Oliver had an attorney who could speak to the charges. Saying he was “extremely disappointed,” the Republican candidate for governor, Mike Minogue, had called on Oliver to suspend his campaign “Shawn is lucky to be alive and lucky that no one innocent was hurt. There is no excuse for driving under the influence,” Minogue said in a statement. He said he’d spoken with Oliver and said “he needs to put his family first,” offering help so that Oliver ensures he doesn’t have another such incident. New Bedford Mayor Jon Mitchell said in a statement he was made aware of the incident this morning and called the allegations against Oliver “deeply concerning,” adding, “the public deserves to hear his explanation of what happened.” The head of the Massachusetts Republican Party, Chairwoman Amy Carnevale, said in a statement Sunday morning, “We just learned of the car accident involving Shawn Oliver. We are awaiting additional information as everyone else.”

articles.title: Mulvaney predicts Wiles is in a ‘powerful place’ in the White House but will leave after midterms
articles.summary: Former White House chief of staff Mick Mulvaney said he expects current chief of staff Susie Wiles to leave her post after the midterm elections, but her departure would be on her own terms after reports suggested she may have lost President Trump’s confidence. “If she leaves, and I think she probably will, it’s not…
articles.body:
Former White House chief of staff Mick Mulvaney said he expects current chief of staff Susie Wiles to leave her post after the midterm elections, but her departure would be on her own terms after reports suggested she may have lost President Trump’s confidence.

“If she leaves, and I think she probably will, it’s not necessarily because she’s fallen out of favor with Trump,” Mulvaney said in an interview with NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday.”

“It’s just a natural sort of time to make that change,” he added.

Mulvaney, who served as Trump’s acting chief of staff during his first term, said Wiles remains an influential figure in the administration despite speculation about her future at the White House.

Speculation over Wiles’s relationship with the president came amid the controversial hiring and quick firing of former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia. Reports suggest Wiles had distanced herself from the decision to bring Zacharia into the administration, which Trump chose to do anyway.

“I think she probably leaked it out that she was not involved in the hiring of Katie Zacharia,” Mulvaney said, describing it as one of the few leaks to emerge from the chief of staff’s office.

Politico reported that Wiles helped set up Zacharia’s Fox News interview with Sean Hannity, where the longtime friend of Trump grilled her about her legal credentials and shaky first press briefing.

Trump reportedly fired Zacharia after watching her interviews with Hannity and on the MAGA-friendly morning show “Fox & Friends,” which a senior White House official described to Politico as “the nail in her coffin” alongside her “her weird answer on being a lawyer.”

Mulvaney noted the subsequent reports of Wiles’s possible involvement in putting Zacharia out of a job, which he viewed as further evidence that she continues to wield considerable influence.

Trump also publicly defended Wiles, dismissing any speculation that her job was in jeopardy.

“TOTAL FAKE NEWS Politico doesn’t care about facts, integrity, or honest journalism — it’s why I kicked them out of the White House!” Trump said in a statement to the outlet. “Susie Wiles is my loyal and longest serving Chief of Staff — there is a reason for that. She has been with me since the beginning, is my trusted advisor, and has my COMPLETE confidence.”

The Washington Post reported Friday that a power struggle has erupted in the White House amid speculation that Wiles may step down from her powerful position.

Several senior administration officials have reportedly begun positioning themselves as potential successors, including deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin and Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte.

articles.title: Nixon defends call to put opponent Moody in jail
articles.summary: Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon defended her recent call to put her GOP opponent Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.) in jail over accusations she approved of mishandling taxpayer funds into a charity called Hope Florida. Appearing on CBS’s “Face the Nation” on Saturday, Nixon was asked whether her calls for Moody to be “locked up and…
articles.body:
Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon defended her recent call to put her GOP opponent Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.) in jail over accusations she approved of mishandling taxpayer funds into a charity called Hope Florida.

Appearing on CBS’s “Face the Nation” on Saturday, Nixon was asked whether her calls for Moody to be “locked up and punished in jail” sounded “like a desire to weaponize the justice system?”

“It’s not a desire to weaponize the justice system. It’s designed to actually hold corrupt politicians accountable for what they’re doing,” Nixon said. “Again, I want an investigation done. I would like the Department of Justice to investigate because nearly $10 million was stolen from sick kids, and people are pointing the finger saying they don’t know who did it, and so we need to bring that in.”

“Look, this is Donald Trump 2.0 here in the state of Florida, and we really need to work to push back. I’m wondering how many kids are going to die because 10 million dollars was taken from Medicaid that was supposed to make sure that those sick kids had the treatment that they needed,” she continued.

Nixon has repeatedly bashed Moody on the welfare scandal as a sealed grand jury report — obtained by CBS News Miami — found $10 million of the total $67 million settlement agreement from the state’s largest Medicaid contractor, Centene, went to Hope Florida as a “donation.”

The report found the money was used by organizations that helped campaign against a Florida ballot measure that would have legalized recreational marijuana in 2024 instead of helping “community-based welfare programs” that were intended to be “a cost-efficient alternative to government assistance programs.”

Moody, who was Florida’s attorney general at the time, was reportedly aware of the plan to divert the payment and “authorized” her former chief deputy attorney general, John Guard, to sign the settlement agreement, according to the grand jury report.

Moody is up for reelection this year after being appointed by Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) to take over Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s seat in the Senate. She faces off against Nixon, a Florida state representative, who won her Democratic primary in a shocking win earlier this year.

Since her primary win, Nixon notched support from key progressive lawmakers — including Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) who campaigned with her last week.

Though Republicans are facing a rocky midterm environment amid growing voter dissatisfaction with the economy, Moody has been maintaining a double-digit lead over Nixon in recent polling.

Moody’s campaign did not respond immediately to The Hill’s request for comment.

articles.title: Newsom campaigns with New Hampshire Democrats ahead of midterms
articles.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) campaigned with Democrats in New Hampshire only a few weeks out from the midterms. “Great to be back in New Hampshire. The energy across the Granite State is UNDENIABLE. Fired-up crowds, incredible volunteers, and so much enthusiasm heading into November 3,” Newsom wrote on social media Sunday. “Grateful to join…
articles.body:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) campaigned with Democrats in New Hampshire only a few weeks out from the midterms.

“Great to be back in New Hampshire. The energy across the Granite State is UNDENIABLE. Fired-up crowds, incredible volunteers, and so much enthusiasm heading into November 3,” Newsom wrote on social media Sunday.

“Grateful to join so many incredible candidates here up and down the ballot. The stakes couldn’t be higher. Get out and VOTE. Let’s TAKE this country BACK,” he added.

Newsom’s post featured photos of him taking part in campaign events alongside Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.), the Democratic candidate in New Hampshire’s Senate race who is facing former Sen. John E. Sununu (R-N.H.) to fill retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen’s (D) seat in the upper chamber.

According to Decision Desk HQ, Pappas has an 84 percent chance of winning, and the nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report rates his race as leaning Democratic.

New Hampshire is one of the earlier states in the 2028 presidential primary calendar for Democrats, and Newsom’s trip to the Granite State may be a sign that he’ll make a 2028 bid for the White House.

Newsom is often floated as a 2028 contender, alongside his fellow Californian former Vice President Kamala Harris and other prominent Democrats including Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (N.Y.).

During President Trump’s second term, Newsom has fashioned himself into an attack dog against the president, taking aim at his social media posting style and calling out the current president over his actions on multiple occasions.

articles.title: This Week on the Hill: Michigan Senate debate, Trump rallies and Obama hits the trail
articles.summary: With just more than two weeks until Election Day, candidates are stepping up their campaigns in a final push to win over voters. In Michigan, Democratic progressive Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers are set to face off Wednesday in a televised debate, hosted by WXYZ-TV. The two candidates are competing…
articles.body:
With just more than two weeks until Election Day, candidates are stepping up their campaigns in a final push to win over voters.

In Michigan, Democratic progressive Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers are set to face off Wednesday in a televised debate, hosted by WXYZ-TV. The two candidates are competing for the open U.S. Senate seat, a contest that will help determine control of the upper chamber.

President Trump will keep up a dynamic travel schedule stumping for GOP candidates, with rallies scheduled in Wichita, Kan., on Monday; Greenville, N.C., on Tuesday; Clemson, S.C., on Wednesday; Sioux City, Iowa, on Thursday; Fort Myers, Fla., on Friday; Georgia on Saturday; and Michigan on Oct. 25. Trump is aiming to boost Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.), Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.), Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa), among others.

Former President Obama, meanwhile, will campaign with El-Sayed in Detroit on Saturday, joining him and other Michigan Democrats at a rally that will also feature Democratic gubernatorial candidate Jocelyn Benson. Obama’s visit will kick off the first day of in-person early voting in the Great Lakes State.

He is also expected to travel to Cleveland on Saturday to stump for Ohio Senate candidate Sherrod Brown (D) and Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton (D).

And former President Clinton will campaign with Democratic candidate David Jolly, who’s running in the Florida gubernatorial race, on Tuesday in Hollywood, Fla.

El-Sayed and Rogers to face off again: El-Sayed has been leading Rogers in polls by several percentage points, as Democrats are looking to flip control of the Senate.

Trump to boost GOP in midterms: Trump’s campaign trips come as Republicans have been confronting voter frustrations over rising gas and grocery prices.

Obama to travel to Michigan and Ohio: Obama will stump for El-Sayed and Brown, both of whom are competing in tough Senate races.

Clinton to stump for Jolly: Jolly is facing off against Republican Rep. Byron Donalds in the Florida gubernatorial race. Donalds has been endorsed by Trump.

El-Sayed and Rogers to spar on the debate stage Wednesday

El-Sayed and Rogers will face off for the second time.

The two had participated in a debate hosted by Nexstar’s Grand Rapids, Mich., station and NewsNation earlier this month, where they lobbed personal attacks centering on corporate and foreign influence, carpetbagging, Trump and their professional careers.

El-Sayed looked to make the debate a referendum on the president by tying Rogers to Trump. The GOP candidate sought to cast himself as bipartisan while characterizing the Democrat as dishonest. Last month, the Democrat took the debate stage alone after Rogers declined to participate, accusing the host outlet of bias.

A Suffolk University poll released last month found that 47 percent of likely Michigan voters would back El-Sayed and 40 percent said they support Rogers in the November contest. A RealClearPolling average of polls between Sept. 24 and Oct. 14 found that El-Sayed is leading Rogers by 2.6 percentage points.

Rogers, who is endorsed by the president, has sought to walk a tightrope with Trump amid his unpopularity. Rogers called for an end to the trade war with Canada, and he previously called for the conflict in Iran to come to an end.

He has also broken with the Trump administration over its immigration crackdown, suggesting in the first debate that actions taken by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Minnesota had gone too far.

Progressive firebrand Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) has been stumping for El-Sayed, even transferring $1 million to him in the final push of the race.

Trump is expected to campaign this week in North Carolina, South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa, Georgia, Michigan and Florida, urging voters to turn out as Republicans grow increasingly concerned about suffering significant losses on Nov. 3.

Sabato’s Crystal Ball, an election handicapper, shifted the Kansas Senate race to a “toss-up” amid growing voter dissatisfaction with the GOP over the economy.

The group noted in its explanation that it was “hesitant” to shift the race, but “a full-on Republican rescue operation appears underway for” Marshall, who is running for his second term against Democrat Adam Hamilton.

In Iowa, Hinson is running a tough race against Democratic candidate Josh Turek for the Iowa Senate seat. Hinson has publicly tried to separate herself from Trump, calling for an immediate end to the Iran war. Cook Political Report refers to Iowa as “ground zero for backlash to the effect of Trump’s tariffs and Iran War on the agriculture industry.”

And Graham is running against Democratic pediatrician Annie Andrews in the South Carolina Senate race. Graham, however, is seen as the favorite to win in November, with Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) forecasting a 70 percent probability that the GOP senator wins next month.

Obama to stump for Democrats in Michigan and Ohio

Obama is slated to travel to Cleveland to stump for Brown and Acton on Saturday. Brown is trying to unseat Sen. Jon Husted (R), who was appointed to the Senate by Gov. Mike DeWine (R) after JD Vance became vice president, while Acton is up against biotech entrepreneur Vivek Ramaswamy to be the state’s chief executive.

In an endorsement video released by Brown’s campaign this month, Obama praised the former U.S. senator for fighting for working people and encouraging job growth during his presidency.

“This race is going to be close,” the former president said in the video. “It could determine which party controls the Senate and whether Ohioans can count on the people in Washington to be fighting for you.”

He will also travel to Detroit in an effort to boost El-Sayed’s campaign. Winning the Michigan Senate seat could be pivotal to Democrats’ hopes of flipping the upper chamber, where they need to net four seats to take control. DDHQ forecasts Democrats have a narrow, 56 percent probability of winning the upper chamber, compared with a 76 percent chance of winning the House.

After Obama’s 2012 election, El-Sayed wrote in a Huffington Post op-ed that “Obama was not the right choice. He just wasn’t the wrong one.” The Michigan Democrat also named off his disagreements with Obama’s record of deportations and expansion of drone warfare in the Middle East, among other criticisms.

But he had addressed that past criticism in an interview with NBC News’s Kristen Welker this month, when he said that he knows “Obama was handed a really difficult set of circumstances, and he did his best.”

El-Sayed also said his campaign and Democratic candidates in 2026 might “push on in different ways than his administration.”

“But it is to say that where we push differently is because we’ve learned from what he’s done and because we stand on the shoulders of giants,” the Michigan Democrat said. “And so, I am so grateful to have been a young man in my 20s with Barack Hussein Obama as president. I would never have seen myself running for office.”

Clinton to campaign for Jolly in Florida

Clinton is slated on Tuesday to stump for Jolly, the Democratic nominee in the Florida gubernatorial race.

Jolly served in the House as a Republican before becoming an independent in 2019, following woes with Trump. He later registered as a Democrat and launched his gubernatorial bid in his new party.

Jolly has previously said he’s not focused on the political divide within the party but rather is seeking solutions to big-ticket issues impacting voters ahead of the midterm elections.

“I’m in a very postpartisan, postideological space. I reject the left-right spectrum. I don’t care about the left-right spectrum. We have big problems that need big solutions. So what I did as a Democrat is amplify the fundamental values in our party, that the economy should work for everybody,” Jolly said on NewsNation’s “Cuomo.”

Several polls have shown Donalds leading Jolly by a wide margin. A Stetson University poll , conducted among 862 likely voters, found that 52 percent would back Donalds, while 41 percent of voters would support Jolly. Three percent said they would back a different candidate, and 5 percent of voters said they were undecided.

Caroline Vakil, Sarah Davis, Julia Mueller and Ryan Mancini contributed.

articles.title: With Ken Paxton’s race faltering, GOP looks for someone to blame
articles.summary: Texas’s Senate race is devolving into a blame game among Republicans weeks out from Election Day as the party’s nominee Ken Paxton faces a stream of negative headlines and Democrats grow increasingly confident about flipping the state. Republican tensions spilled into the public on Thursday when President Trump lashed out at incumbent Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and…
articles.body:
Texas’s Senate race is devolving into a blame game among Republicans weeks out from Election Day as the party’s nominee Ken Paxton faces a stream of negative headlines and Democrats grow increasingly confident about flipping the state.

Republican tensions spilled into the public on Thursday when President Trump lashed out at incumbent Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and veteran GOP strategist Karl Rove on Truth Social, accusing them of working to undermine Paxton.

The Texas attorney general has been hit recently with a near-constant stream of negative headlines and declining poll numbers, presenting Democrats with a potential pickup opportunity.

“Trump ought to be encouraging turnout in Texas instead of laying blame on an outgoing senator,” said Chad Wilbanks, a Texas-based lobbyist and former executive director of the state’s Republican Party.

“It’s the name calling, it’s the bashing,” he continued, saying it’s coming from populist Republicans in Paxton’s coalition of supporters. “It really turns a lot of voters off, quite candidly.”

“They’re tired of the name-calling. They’re tired of the blaming,” he said.

The president on Thursday said that Cornyn, who lost to Paxton in a tense primary runoff, and Rove, former President George W. Bush’s White House adviser, “are doing everything possible to make it hard” for Paxton.

Since his primary loss to Paxton in May, Cornyn has not campaigned alongside him, and Rove has backed a Democrat in a downballot race.

“The primary wounds still haven’t healed,” said Dan Eberhart, a Paxton donor, describing the dynamic as “McConnell versus MAGA.”

Cornyn’s 2014 campaign manager, Brendan Steinhauser, dismissed the notion that his former boss was behind any intraparty sniping ahead of Election Day.

“This is an indication that he thinks it’s very possible that Paxton could lose, and that he wants to make sure he gets ahead of that story, and says ‘this is not my fault. I did everything I could to help Ken Paxton,'” Steinhauser said.

“If Sen. Cornyn had this much political power and influence, he would have simply reelected himself,” he said.

When asked for his response to the president’s comments, Cornyn’s former senior campaign adviser Matt Mackowick quoted a line from the 1996 action move “The Rock.”

“Losers always b—- about having their best. Winners go out and f— the prom queen,” Mackowick said.

Republicans have the homefield advantage in Texas, which voted for Trump by big margins in each of his three presidential elections, and where the GOP has dominated statewide seats for decades.

But Paxton’s controversy-laden bid, coupled with a strong campaign from Talarico, has put Republicans on defense in the red stronghold.

Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) rates the race a toss-up, with Talarico narrowly favored to win. After three new polls last week showed the Democrat leading Paxton, Talarico is leading by 2 percentage points in DDHQ’s polling averages.

Trump made Paxton a focus of both of his addresses at the RNC’s midterm convention last month in Dallas, and the president and vice president have both visited the state multiple times since to rally Texas Republicans.

Paxton, though, said the convention “dropped our numbers,” according to audio leaked by the New York Times last month, which was among a string of leaks that have ruffled Republicans.

Politico also obtained audio in which Paxton admitted that his Texas campaign is being run by Washington, saying, “I’ve never been in a race where I felt less control over the campaign.” And in a clip obtained by Axios, Paxton said affordability is “why we’re having a hard time with numbers.”

As Paxton trails in the polls, money is flooding into the race.

Talarico reported a staggering $64 million haul this summer, saying it’s the biggest third-quarter pull by any Senate candidate.

Paxton reported $18 million in the same period. Trump’s MAGA Inc. dropped $10 million into the race in early September, and tech mogul Elon Musk poured $158 million into a super PAC backing the Republican, according to new filings.

Total ad spending has topped $500 million, according to AdImpact, with Republican advertisers accounting for more than half that amount.

Spending has been a source of debate among Republicans, with some arguing that Trump’s super PAC MAGA Inc. waited too long to put their massive war chest to use in the state.

“I wish they would have started earlier,” Eberhart said. “I think the cavalry arrived just in the nick of time.”

Republicans predict that Paxton will see a boost in the polls given the flood of cash meant to support him in the race.

“Ultimately, we think we will be successful,” said one GOP source.

But not all Republicans are as optimistic that money alone can save Paxton. Some say he may have to ultimately rely on the state’s incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott (R), who is facing a competitive reelection bid himself.

“It’s on Abbott to carry Paxton over the finish line,” Eberhart said. “And if he wins, he owes Abbott a Texas-sized thank-you card.”

But Abbott is largely running his own state-level race and has the advantage of being at least somewhat more insulated from the woes facing federal Republican candidates.

Abbott notably did not campaign with Trump and Paxton last week in San Antonio, citing a scheduling conflict.

Against that backdrop, Paxton has also ignored calls from both Talarico and Trump for a debate between the Senate rivals.

The three-term attorney general avoided debating his Democratic opponents during each of his runs for the top prosecutor’s office, but this year’s Senate race is a more high-profile, neck-and-neck contest.

“I don’t think Ken Paxton’s ever debated, so it’s not really a shock that that has kind of continued. And it just means that he probably doesn’t think that he’s the best debater, and it’s not one of his strong suits,” said Aaron Kall, the director of debate at the University of Michigan and the editor of several books about political debates and speeches.

Trump has openly and repeatedly said that he doesn’t “like the way Ken dresses,” “talks” or “looks,” even as he urges voters to back the Senate hopeful.

Paxton may be weighing the “opportunity cost” to participate against Talarico, whose speaking style has been hailed by his own party, Kall said.

But there’s also a downside to not stepping on the debate stage, Kall added. “Generally, it’s a sign of weakness in that you’re kind of declining this invitation or opportunity, and [can] mean you’re not really comfortable in your skills and ability to articulate positions and defend yourself.”

Talarico debated Texas voters in a solo appearance at a CNN-Jubilee town hall last week, with the outlet noting that Paxton had yet to respond to the invitation to participate.

When Talarico was away from the campaign trail with the flu at the start of the month, according to the campaign, Trump said on Truth Social that the Democrat should “immediately report to a debate stage” against Paxton, who he said was “ready, willing, and able.”

Rep. Brandon Gill (R-Texas), a top Paxton surrogate, said on Fox News on Thursday that a debate “would certainly be enlightening” and that he’d “love to see that contrast in front of voters very clear.”

“I guess this is just the Sturm und Drang of a competitive, close Senate race,” Texas Republican consultant Vinny Minchillo said of Trump’s finger-pointing amid the fundraising surge and tight polling.

“Should Paxton lose — not so sure he’s going to — plenty of blame to go around.”

articles.title: Bessent says there was no sanctions relief for Russia after U.S. diesel deal
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday said President Trump did not provide Russia with sanctions relief by waiving sanctions against Russia set to take effect soon, after signing off on a deal that allows Russia to permit diesel into the U.S. and global marketplace. NBC News’s Kristen Welker on “Meet the Press” pressed Bessent on…
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday said President Trump did not provide Russia with sanctions relief by waiving sanctions against Russia set to take effect soon, after signing off on a deal that allows Russia to permit diesel into the U.S. and global marketplace.

NBC News’s Kristen Welker on “Meet the Press” pressed Bessent on Trump’s waiver and asked what Russian President Vladimir Putin has “done to deserve sanctions relief now.”

“Well, first of all Kristen, that’s not true. No sanctions were lifted on Friday. No sanctions were lifted,” Bessent answered.

Welker asked if U.S. sanctions on Russia will be lifted.

“There is a 60-day period so we can examine what’s going on,” the Treasury secretary said. “The only thing that has been lifted is the diesel embargo. And, I will point out –– the U.K. in May waived their embargo on diesel and jet fuel made with Russian crude. So, you know, where’s the outrage for the rest of the world?”

Bessent accused Ukraine’s European partners of “financing the Russian war machine,” adding that European countries import 10 times more than the $4 billion that the U.S. imports from Russian products.

He said it was a “false binary” to say the U.S. is siding with Russia in its war with Ukraine, which the U.S. has pledged support for since Russia invaded in 2022.

When asked by Welker if the U.S. is still an ally to Ukraine, Bessent said Trump seeks to bring the war to an end.

And [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelensky presents a false binary this morning that Ukraine must win,” Bessent said, referring to Welker’s earlier interview with Zelensky in the broadcast. “The war must end, and that will be with some kind of a negotiated settlement, and President Trump is working on that every day. He’s done it since he came into office.”

Welker asked Bessent the same question two more times, prompting Bessent to say that “I’m not the secretary of state. I’m not the president.”

Trump officially signed a sanctions package into law last month. It seeks to put pressure on the Kremlin to end its years-long military operations against Ukraine by imposing tariffs on top Russian energy purchasers and those who help the country evade sanctions.

The waiver comes after the diesel deal, part of the administration’s efforts to lower fuel prices, which have risen amid the U.S.’s war in Iran. Both the deal and the waiver come weeks before the November midterm elections.

But Trump’s deal sparked backlash from bipartisan members of Congress. Five Republican lawmakers joined their Democratic colleagues to denounce the relief. Bessent was copied, along with Secretary of State Marco Rubio, on the lawmakers’ letter urging Trump to reconsider.

One of the lawmakers, Rep. Michael McCaul (R-Texas), the former chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said separately that he understands Trump’s intent to lower diesel fuel prices, but said he was “concerned” that the deal “will only fuel the Kremlin’s violence and destruction.”

articles.title: US Chamber of Commerce endorses Paxton over Talarico
articles.summary: The U.S. Chamber of Commerce announced it endorsed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton over Democrat James Talarico in the state’s battleground Senate contest ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. “The choice is clear in Texas. Attorney General Ken Paxton has been a defender of free enterprise and the pro-growth policies that empower American businesses to…
articles.body:
The U.S. Chamber of Commerce announced it endorsed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton over Democrat James Talarico in the state’s battleground Senate contest ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.

“The choice is clear in Texas. Attorney General Ken Paxton has been a defender of free enterprise and the pro-growth policies that empower American businesses to thrive,” Neil Bradley, Executive Vice President and Chief Policy Officer of the Chamber of Commerce, said in a statement . “He has pushed back against federal overreach, helped preserve a low-tax environment, and defended the energy sector from burdensome mandates.”

“Paxton understands that true economic prosperity relies on a fair and predictable justice system. We look forward to working together on meaningful legal reform that shields job creators from lawsuit abuse and red tape,” Bradley concluded.

Paxton, a Trump-endorsed candidate, ousted Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) in a Republican primary runoff in May but since then has struggled to build a lead against Talarico amid dissatisfaction with the GOP in the Lone Star State.

Cook Political Report shifted the race away from Republicans to a “ toss-up ” rating in August. Decision Desk HQ, a partner of The Hill, designated the race as a coin flip but narrowly favoring Democrats, giving Talarico a 54 percent probability of flipping the seat.

Talarico has also hammered Paxton on his controversial record as the Lone Star State’s top prosecutor who was impeached by the Texas state House in 2023 before being acquitted by the state Senate — and, in audio shared by The New York Times, Paxton contended that his appearance at the GOP’s midterm convention “ dropped our numbers .”

The Chamber of Commerce has been active for over 100 years and previously clashed with the Trump administration earlier this year over enacting tariffs against nearly every country.

The Chamber of Commerce opposed President Trump’s tariffs in an amicus brief in a Supreme Court case last year arguing the president was overstepping his statutory authority and his actions were causing “irreparable harm to businesses of all sizes.”

The Supreme Court later ruled the tariffs were unlawful and rejected Trump’s expanded use of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) in imposing tariffs.

After the ruling, Bradley wrote in another statement that the Chamber of Commerce encouraged “the administration to use this opportunity to reset overall tariff policy in a manner that will lead to greater economic growth, larger wage gains for workers, and lower costs for families.”

articles.title: El-Sayed criticizes implications of ‘Muslim Brotherhood’ question
articles.summary: Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed criticized the implications of a question asked at a Saturday town hall concerning the Muslim Brotherhood. At a campaign event in Michigan, El-Sayed was asked by an attendee whether he would “disavow the Muslim Brotherhood.” “Sure. Yeah, absolutely,” El-Sayed said. “Why are you asking the question?” In the 4…
articles.body:
Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed criticized the implications of a question asked at a Saturday town hall concerning the Muslim Brotherhood.

At a campaign event in Michigan, El-Sayed was asked by an attendee whether he would “disavow the Muslim Brotherhood.”

“Sure. Yeah, absolutely,” El-Sayed said. “Why are you asking the question?”

In the 4 minute clip of the exchange shared on X, El-Sayed continued to ask the implications behind the question, adding, “have you asked everybody in your life if they disavow them? So why are you asking me?”

He continued that the attendee was assuming, “because I am Muslim, that somehow, I would have some allegiance to something that is not our constitution. That’s your assumption. That’s implicit in the question.”

El-Sayed described similar questions being asked to former President John F. Kennedy regarding his faith as he served as the country’s first Catholic president and whether his allegiance would be to the Pope and the Vatican.

“And [Kennedy’s] answer, famously, was that he was not running to be a Catholic president. He was running to be president and happened to be Catholic,” he recalled. “I’m not running to be a Muslim senator, I’m running for U.S. Senate and happen to be Muslim.”

“And the reality of it is this: I’m never going to tell you what faith you can or can’t practice. I want to protect your right to practice your faith as you choose,” El-Sayed concluded.

He is facing former Rep. Mike Rogers (R) in a competitive Senate contest to replace retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D). The seat is one the GOP hopes to flip in its effort to retain control of the upper chamber.

Rogers previously alleged during a candidate debate that El-Sayed and his family have ties to the Muslim Brotherhood – citing political contributions to El-Sayed from individuals connected to the group and previously claimed the Democrat “pledged his support” to the organization.

The Muslim Brotherhood is an Islamist religiopolitical organization that was founded in Egypt in 1928 that resulted in political factions in the Middle East and extremist groups like Hamas, according to Britannica .

Bridge Michigan reported last month that there was no evidence that El-Sayed has direct ties to or pledged support to the group.

During the same debate, El-Sayed slammed Rogers for his ties to the Trump administration which the former lawmaker has attempted to distance himself from by calling for the war in Iran to end and calling for the tariff war with Canada to be resolved.

Decision Desh HQ, a partner of The Hill, predicted the battleground Senate election leaning in favor of El-Sayed, forecasting him with a 68 percent chance of winning. While Cook Political Report rated the race as a “toss up” with both parties equal on its partisan voting index.

articles.summary: Comedian and satirist Nathan Fielder’s documentary about Elizabeth Holmes drew 2,000 sold-out shows in its limited release across the United States. articles.body:
Comedian and satirist Nathan Fielder’s documentary about Elizabeth Holmes drew 2,000 sold-out shows in its limited release across the United States.

The documentary – called “You Can See Everything” – was released on 855 screens over the weekend, with sold-out shows showing the nearly three-hour film that was expected to focus on Holmes’s life before she reported to prison in 2023.

It grossed an estimated $15 million over the weekend, according to Forbes , with an expected expanded release into more theaters next week.

Holmes is currently in federal prison for lying to investors about the capabilities of her blood-testing technology. While working as the founder of Theranos, she claimed the company’s blood-testing technology could perform several diagnostic tests with only one drop of blood.

At the time, the Stanford dropout was heralded as the next Steve Jobs, whom she admired and modeled herself after.

The scheme drew in several major figures, including media mogul Rupert Murdoch and former Education Secretary Betsy DeVos, to invest in Theranos. Former Secretaries of State Henry Kissinger and George Shultz also sat on the company’s board.

Federal regulators announced in 2024 that Holmes had also been banned from participating in federal health programs for 90 years – essentially meaning she will not be able to work for an entity that receives federal healthcare funding apart from some limited circumstances.

Though she might be eligible to receive federal health benefits after she finishes her prison sentence.

Theranos COO Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani, whom Holmes had a relationship with as they ran the company, had already been excluded from federal programs, also for 90 years. Holmes has also accused Balwani of rape since the company’s downfall.

articles.title: Troy Jackson doesn’t regret telling opponent Susan Collins to ‘shut up’
articles.summary: Democrat Troy Jackson said on Sunday he does not regret telling his opponent Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) to “shut up” during a candidate debate that was interrupted by an anti-data center protester. During an interview on CNN’s “State of the Union,” host Dana Bash asked Jackson whether he regretted the comment. “No, you know she…
articles.body:
Democrat Troy Jackson said on Sunday he does not regret telling his opponent Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) to “shut up” during a candidate debate that was interrupted by an anti-data center protester.

During an interview on CNN’s “ State of the Union ,” host Dana Bash asked Jackson whether he regretted the comment.

“No, you know she said that it was a Troy supporter. I mean, she accused me of setting that up. I had no idea who it was,” he said. “I mean, I was surprised whenever he jumped up out of there.”

“You know, I’ve had four debates with Senator Collins. I shook her hand afterwards every time. But what I’m not going to be is, you know, talked down to by Senator Collins, I’m not going to be accused of things like that,” he continued, adding that he was “fighting for Mainers and I just think that was another situation where she was talking down to me and I’m not going to apologize for that.”

The incident happened when an anti-data center protester interrupted a debate. Collins said almost immediately as the debate was stalled, “So, this is obviously one of Troy’s supporters.”

Jackson interjected, “Oh, shut up. I don’t even know that kid.”

The anti-data center protester confirmed on Saturday he had “zero coordination” with Jackson’s campaign, adding that he did “not know Troy Jackson personally or at all…but I think he should be winning,” according to the New York Times .

Collins discussed the incident on Fox News , telling Sean Hannity she was “struck by how reflective the response, ‘Oh, shut up,’ was.”

“But then I thought about the reputation that Troy Jackson has in Augusta particularly when he’s dealing with women with whom he disagrees. So, in some ways it didn’t surprise me,” she added.

The Maine Democrat discussed this “reputation” further with Bash detailing stories from GOP members alleging that during his tenure as President of Maine’s state Senate, Jackson was “sort of aggressive in [his] tone” to women.

“Some Republicans have been spending millions of dollars attacking me and my family, making untrue claims, things that they had to take off the air, and so it doesn’t surprise me that some Republicans would be making any claims,” Jackson responded.

The Maine Senate contest is one race Democrats hope to pick up in their effort to regain control of the upper chamber. Jackson leads Collins with a razor-thin margin in a recent Suffolk University poll , but since the result is within the margin of error, both candidates are statistically tied.
